title: Hormonal contraceptives and performance
goal: Name the main types of hormonal contraception, say how the combined pill changes hormones, and weigh what the 2020 meta-analysis shows about performance.

steps.title: Types of hormonal contraception
steps.text:
[Hormonal contraceptives](g:hormonal-contraceptive) include pills, implants, injections, hormone-releasing coils (IUDs), vaginal rings and patches [[c:fem-hc-types]]. The copper coil has no hormones.

Two features matter in research:

- **Which hormones.** The [combined pill](g:combined-pill) has a man-made oestrogen plus a [progestin](g:progestin). Progestin-only methods (some pills, implants, injections, hormonal coils) have no oestrogen.
- **How the dose is given.** In mono-, bi- or triphasic pills the dose stays the same or changes in two or three steps across the pack.

Formulation and length of use vary widely [[c:fem-formulation]], so 'the pill' is not one exposure. The meta-analysis in this lesson covers oral contraceptives.

claims.text: Hormonal contraceptives include oral pills, implants, injections, hormone-releasing coils, vaginal rings and patches; copper coils are not hormonal.

evidence.quote: Report the type (e.g., OCPs, implants, injections, intrauterine devices/coils that are hormone releasing and NOT copper-based, vaginal rings, contraceptive transdermal patches)

claims.text: Oral contraceptives differ in oestrogen and progestin formulation and dose, in how the dose changes, and in duration of use.

evidence.quote: The researcher will also need to consider the type of OCP being used (i.e., oestrogen and progestin formulations and concentrations; monophasic, biphasic, triphasic) and the duration of usage

steps.title: A double agent, and the withdrawal bleed
steps.text:
The combined pill is a 'double agent': it *lowers* the body's own oestrogen (oestradiol) and progesterone and at the same time *adds* man-made oestrogen and progestin on active-pill days [[c:fem-double]]. A pill user has a flat, different hormone profile, not a natural cycle.

The bleed in the pill-free or placebo days is a [withdrawal bleed](g:withdrawal-bleed), not a true period. Researchers use that word so pill users do not count as eumenorrheic just because they bleed regularly. In those inactive days the body's own hormones rise again [[c:fem-withdrawal]]. A regular withdrawal bleed also says little about whether the natural cycle works, which matters for [REDs](g:reds) screening.

claims.text: Oral contraceptives lower the body's own oestradiol and progesterone while supplying man-made oestrogen and progestin on active days.

evidence.quote: Oral contraceptive pills (OCPs) are double agents, which downregulate endogenous concentrations of oestradiol and progesterone whilst simultaneously providing daily supplementation of exogenous oestrogen and progestin during the OCP-taking days.

claims.text: Pill users should not be labelled eumenorrheic on bleeding patterns; their own hormones rise during the pill-free days.

evidence.quote: Stop OCP users misidentifying themselves as eumenorrheic based on bleeding patterns
The endogenous concentration of oestrogen and progesterone rises during the OCP free/inactive/placebo days

steps.title: What the meta-analysis found
steps.text:
Elliott-Sale and colleagues pooled 42 studies of 590 women [[c:fem-ocp-perf]]. They compared pill users with naturally cycling women, and pill-taking days with pill-free days.

- Users vs natural cycles: performance was perhaps slightly lower on average, but any group effect was most likely trivial.
- Pill days vs pill-free days: almost no chance of even a small effect either way.
- Performance was steady across the pill cycle.

Of the studies, 83% were of moderate, low or very low quality [[c:fem-ocp-quality]]. The authors found no basis for general advice for or against the pill; where performance matters most, an individual approach fits [[c:fem-ocp-individual]].

claims.text: Oral contraceptive users may perform slightly worse on average than naturally cycling women, but any group effect is most likely trivial, and performance is steady across the pill cycle.

evidence.quote: OCP use might result in slightly inferior exercise performance on average when compared to naturally menstruating women, although any group-level effect is most likely to be trivial.
The analysis also indicated that exercise performance was consistent across the OCP cycle.

claims.text: Most of the included studies were of moderate, low or very low quality.

evidence.quote: Most studies (83%) were graded as moderate, low or very low quality, with 17% achieving high quality.

claims.text: The evidence does not justify general advice on pill use compared with non-use.

evidence.quote: the current evidence does not warrant general guidance on OCP use compared with non-use

steps.title: Why pill studies are hard to read
steps.text:
Three problems affect pill research.

1. **Matching.** To compare users with natural cycles you must pick a phase. Pill-free days against early bleeding pit two similar, low-hormone states; active pill days against the mid-luteal phase pit different ones [[c:fem-match]]. The 2020 review matched both ways (pill-free days with early bleeding, active pill days with the other phases); in both, a small effect was unlikely [[c:fem-ocp-match]].
2. **Pooling.** Different pills, doses and years of use go into one group.
3. **Words.** Calling pill days 'the early follicular phase' gives pill users cycle labels they do not have [[c:fem-language]].

So a result about 'the pill' says little about one specific method in one woman.

claims.text: Which cycle phase pill users are compared with decides how similar the hormone environments are.

evidence.quote: if the non-active pill phase is compared with the early follicular phase, then it is likely that the hormonal environments will be very similar between the two groups
If the mid-luteal phase is compared with the active pill phase, the hormonal environments between groups will be different.

claims.text: Cycle phase names should not be applied to pill users, to avoid confusion between users and non-users.

evidence.quote: Prevent confusion between hormonal contraceptive users and non-users

claims.text: The 2020 meta-analysis compared pill users with naturally cycling women in two matchings, and neither made a small performance effect likely.

evidence.quote: For the between-group analysis, women were phase matched in two ways: (1) OCP withdrawal versus the early follicular phase of the menstrual cycle and (2) OCP consumption versus all phases of the menstrual cycle except for the early follicular phase.
OCP use might result in slightly inferior exercise performance on average when compared to naturally menstruating women, although any group-level effect is most likely to be trivial.

points: Hormonal contraception covers pills, implants, injections, hormonal coils, rings and patches; the copper coil has no hormones.
The combined pill lowers the body's own hormones and adds man-made ones; its bleed is a withdrawal bleed, not a period.
A meta-analysis of 42 studies (590 women) found a most likely trivial group effect of the pill on performance, from mostly low-quality studies.
The evidence gives no general case for or against the pill; decide on health first and test your own response if performance is a goal.

variants.stem: Which of these contraceptives has no hormones?

options.text: The copper coil
options.why: Right: it works without hormones.

options.text: The vaginal ring
options.why: The ring releases hormones.

options.text: The implant
options.why: The implant releases a progestin.

options.text: The patch
options.why: The patch releases hormones through the skin.

variants.stem: A cyclist uses a hormone-releasing coil with no oestrogen. Which description fits?

options.text: A progestin-only hormonal contraceptive
options.why: Right: the coil releases a progestin and no oestrogen.

options.text: A combined pill
options.why: The combined pill has both a man-made oestrogen and a progestin.

options.text: A non-hormonal copper method
options.why: Only the copper coil has no hormones.

options.text: A natural cycle
options.why: A hormonal coil is a contraceptive, so her hormone profile is not natural.

variants.stem: Why is the combined pill called a "double agent"?

options.text: It lowers the body's own hormones and adds man-made ones
options.why: Right: both effects at once.

options.text: It both starts and stops ovulation within a day
options.why: The pill suppresses ovulation; it does not start it.

options.text: It acts on both the brain and the legs
options.why: The name refers to the two hormone effects, not two organs.

options.text: It is taken for two cycles at a time
options.why: The name has nothing to do with the schedule.

variants.stem: A runner on the combined pill says she is eumenorrheic because she bleeds every 28 days. What is the best correction?

options.text: It is a withdrawal bleed, so she is a pill user
options.why: Right: the bleed comes from the pill-free days, and pill users should not be called eumenorrheic on bleeding alone.

options.text: Correct: any 28-day bleed shows ovulation
options.why: The pill suppresses ovulation, yet the bleed still happens.

options.text: Wrong: pill users never bleed
options.why: Most combined pills produce a bleed in the pill-free days.

options.text: She is amenorrhoeic because the pill stops periods
options.why: She bleeds, so amenorrhoea does not describe her.

variants.stem: A triathlete on the combined pill has regular bleeds. What does this say about whether her own cycle works, a question that matters for low energy availability?

options.text: Little: the pill sets her bleeding pattern
options.why: Right: whatever her ovaries do, the withdrawal bleed hides the state of the natural cycle.

options.text: That her energy availability is adequate
options.why: Nothing about the bleed shows her energy availability.

options.text: That she ovulates normally on active pills
options.why: The pill is meant to suppress ovulation.

options.text: That her own hormones are at peak levels
options.why: The pill lowers the body's own hormones.

variants.stem: What did the 2020 meta-analysis conclude about the group-level effect of the oral contraceptive pill on performance?

options.text: Most likely trivial, perhaps slightly lower on average
options.why: Right: the authors found no basis for general advice.

options.text: A large improvement
options.why: The probability of even a small benefit was effectively zero.

options.text: A large impairment
options.why: The group-level effect was most likely trivial, not large.

options.text: A clear benefit during pill-free days
options.why: Pill days vs pill-free days showed almost no chance of a small effect.

variants.stem: A cyclist asks whether to stop her pill to raise her FTP. What is the best answer from this evidence?

options.text: No general case to stop; decide with a doctor, health first
options.why: Right: performance effects were trivial on average, and an individual approach is advised.

options.text: Yes: the pill clearly lowers performance
options.why: The group effect was most likely trivial.

options.text: Yes: pill-free days gave much better performance
options.why: Pill days and pill-free days showed almost no chance of a small effect.

options.text: No: the pill clearly raises performance
options.why: The review found no benefit for users.

variants.stem: What limits the comparison of pill users with naturally cycling women?

options.text: Women are not randomly assigned, and most of the studies were of low quality
options.why: Right: users may differ in other ways, and 83% of studies were moderate to very low quality.

options.text: Different tests were used, so no effect could be pooled
options.why: Converting results to effect sizes lets a meta-analysis pool different tests; that is not the main limit.

options.text: Pill users were tested only on pill-free days
options.why: Studies tested pill-taking days too; the review compared both.

options.text: The review used a frequentist method
options.why: The method was Bayesian, and that is not the limit here.

variants.stem: Researchers compare pill-free days with the early follicular phase of naturally cycling women. Why might hormone levels look alike?

options.text: Both are low-hormone states
options.why: Right: the body's own hormones are low in both.

options.text: Both include the progesterone peak
options.why: The progesterone peak is in the mid-luteal phase.

options.text: The pill adds a lot of oestrogen in the pill-free days
options.why: Man-made hormones are taken on the active days.

options.text: Both are the follicular phase by definition
options.why: Pill-free days are not a follicular phase; the match is by hormone level.

variants.stem: A review pools all pill types and reports a trivial effect. A triathlete uses a progestin-only implant and wonders if this applies. What is the best reading?

options.text: Only loosely: it covered oral pills, not her method
options.why: Right: the review pooled oral pill formulations, so her method was probably not studied; formulation and method matter, and an implant is not a pill.

options.text: It applies exactly, as all contraceptives work the same
options.why: Formulations differ widely.

options.text: It does not apply: implants raise performance
options.why: Nothing in the review shows implants raise performance.

options.text: It applies only on the days she is bleeding
options.why: Implants have no pill cycle, and the result is not tied to bleeding days.
